units.la: Theses de Actionibus Ser; vitutum, Confessoria, & Negatoria.
units.tr: Theses on the Actions of Servitudes, Confessory and Negatory.

units.la: I,
units.tr: I,

units.la: CUm de omni Jure in rem, tum de Seruitutibus quoque, Actiones in rem competunt.
units.tr: Since actions in rem lie for every right in rem, so also actions in rem lie for servitudes.

units.la: §. Aeque, Inst. de Act. l. 2. & 6. § hæc autem Actio. D. Si Ser. vind.
units.tr: §. Aeque, Inst. de Act. l. 2. & 6. § hæc autem Actio. D. Si Ser. vind.

units.la: II,
units.tr: II,

units.la: Et quidem de Seruitutibus duæ, Confessoria, & Negatoria: Confessoria ei, qui Seruitutem vel ius ad se pertinere dicit: Negatoria ei, qui Seruitutem vel ius se alteri debere, aut esse negat.
units.tr: There are two actions for servitudes, the confessory and the negatory. The confessory lies for the one who says that the servitude or right belongs to him; the negatory for the one who denies that he owes a servitude or right to another, or that it exists.

units.la: d. § Aeque, d.l. 21[?]
units.tr: d. § Aeque, d.l. 21[?]

units.la: III,[?]
units.tr: III,[?]

units.la: Harum enim Actionum apellationes non a re, ut plerique interpretes putant, sed ab ipsa orationis forma, vel aientis, vel negantis, mihi sumptæ videntur. V.G. his verbis, Aio mihi jus esse, te inuito ædes meas altius tollere, Cōfessoria intenditur:{1} Contra, istis, Nego tibi jus esse, vel Aio tibi jus non esse, inuito me altius tollere ædes tuas, Negatoria.{2}
units.tr: For I think the names of these actions were taken not from the thing, as most interpreters suppose, but from the very form of words, whether affirming or denying. For example, with these words, "I assert that I have the right to raise my building higher, against your will," the confessory is brought. On the other hand, with these, "I deny that you have the right, or I assert that you have no right, to raise your building higher against my will," the negatory.

units.la: {1} d. § Aeque. vers. veluti si quis agat ius &.
units.tr: {1} d. § Aeque. vers. veluti si quis agat ius &.

units.la: {2} d. § Aeque. vers. ut si quis intendat ius non esse ei altius tollendi.
units.tr: {2} d. § Aeque. vers. as if someone should claim the right that he may not build higher.

units.la: IIII,
units.tr: IIII,

units.la: Induxit illos id potissimum, ni fallor, quod de Seruitute Altius non tollendi, fecerint duas, unam Altius tollendi, alteram Altius non tollendi.
units.tr: What led them to this, I think, above all, is that concerning the servitude of not raising higher, they made two: one of raising higher, the other of not raising higher.

units.la: De hac opinione Interpretum alias latius explicabitur, Deo adiuvante.
units.tr: This opinion of the interpreters will be explained more fully elsewhere, God willing.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Sunt autem hae Actiones Ciuiles: & proinde iure Ciuili & sua natura perpetuae. Sed ex Constitutionibus hodie longo tempore pereunt,
units.tr: These actions are civil, and therefore by civil law and by their nature perpetual. But by constitutions they nowadays perish after a long time.

units.la: l. pe. C. de Vsufr. l. pe. C. de seruit. initio tit. Inst. de perp. et temp.
units.tr: l. pe. C. de Vsufr. l. pe. C. de seruit. initio tit. Inst. de perp. et temp.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Et quia de Seruitutibus praediorum, siue potius, de earum Actionibus iam disputamus, Dantur hae Actiones, Directae quidem Domino:{1} Utiles vero, non Domino, ius tamen aliquod in rem habenti, ut Superficiario, Emphyteutae, Creditori pignoratitio:{2} olim quoq; possessori praedij provincialis:{3} hodie vasallo, quem vocant.
units.tr: Since we are now discussing servitudes of estates, or rather their actions, these actions are given: directly indeed to the owner; but in the utile form to one who has some right in the thing without being owner, such as the superficiary, the emphyteuta, the creditor holding a pledge; formerly also to the possessor of a provincial estate; nowadays to the vassal, as they call him.

units.la: {1} l. 1. §. 1. l. 2. §. 1. l. 6. §. haec autem D. Si fer. uind.
units.tr: {1} l. 1. §. 1. l. 2. §. 1. l. 6. §. haec autem D. Si fer. uind.

units.tr: {2} l. 16. ei qui pignori. D. de Seruit. l. 1. §. ult. D. de Superf.

units.la: {3} Arg. l. 3. C de Ser. Lib. 2. Feud. tit. 8. uerf. Rei autem.
units.tr: {3} Arg. l. 3. C de Ser. Lib. 2. Feud. tit. 8. uerf. Rei autem.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Nam et de omni Seruitute, quae iure Praetorio, & non ipso iure constituta est, Utiles tantum accommodari solent.
units.tr: For on every servitude established by praetorian law, and not by the law itself, only utile actions are usually granted.

units.la: d. l. 1. §. ult. D. de Superfic. l. 10. Siquis diuturno. D. Si ser. uind.
units.tr: d. l. 1. §. ult. D. de Superfic. l. 10. Siquis diuturno. D. Si ser. uind.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Fructuario an dentur, controuersum est. Puto ei, suo nomine non dari.{1} potest tamen Vsumfructum vindicare, etiam Seruitutis nomine: de qua & Interdictum habet, ut de Itinere.{2}
units.tr: Whether they are given to the usufructuary is disputed. I think not in his own name. He may however claim the usufruct, even in the name of a servitude, for which he also has an interdict, as for a right of way.

units.la: {1} l. 2. §. 2. et 3. D. Si ser. uind. l. 1. §. 1. D. de Remiss. l. 1. D. Si Vsusf. pet.
units.tr: {1} l. 2. §. 2. et 3. D. Si ser. uind. l. 1. §. 1. D. de Remiss. l. 1. D. Si Vsusf. pet.

units.la: {2} ff. s. utifrui. §. 1. D. Si Vsusf. pet. d. l. 2. §. 3.
units.tr: {2} ff. s. utifrui. §. 1. D. Si Vsusf. pet. d. l. 2. §. 3.

units.la: VIIII.
units.tr: VIIII.

units.la: Dantur autem non tantum contra Dominum, sed etiam contra quemlibet possessorem: atq; adeo contra quemuis alium, um, qui vel Seruitutis vsum, vel rei nostrae, quam sibi seruire existimet, Libertatem impediat.
units.tr: They are given not only against the owner but against any possessor, and indeed against any other person who impedes the use of a servitude, or the freedom of our property which he thinks is subject to a servitude to him.

units.la: d. l. 10. Si quis diuturno. infi. l. 4. §. ult. l. 9. et l. si altius. D. Si ser. uind.
units.tr: d. l. 10. Si quis diuturno. infra l. 4. §. ult. l. 9. et l. si altius. D. Si servitus vindicetur.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Excipitur Seruitus Oneris ferendi: de qua Seruitute, Actio non aduersus alium quam Dominum competit.{1} Ratio Exceptionis, quia singulare ius est huius Seruitutis, ut is qui eam debet, facere quoque aliquid cogatur, puta reficere parietem. at reficere solus dominus potest.{2}
units.tr: The servitude of bearing a burden is an exception: against this servitude an action lies only against the owner, and not against anyone else.{1} The reason for the exception is that this servitude has the peculiar feature that the one who owes it is also compelled to do something, for example to repair the wall; but only the owner can repair it.{2}

units.la: {1} l. 4. §. 6. haec autem actio D. Si ser. uind.
units.tr: {1} l. 4. §. 6. haec autem actio D. Si ser. uind.

units.la: {2} d. l. 6. §. etiam l. 33. cum. D. de. Ser. Vrb.
units.tr: {2} d. l. 6. §. etiam l. 33. cum. D. de. Ser. Vrb.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Socio quidem contra socium hae Actiones in re communi non dantur: sed Communi diuidundo experiri possunt: qua Actione agi potest, nō, Socio ius esse opus facere, sed ius non esse, aut opus facere, aut factum, sed socio absente, ita habere.
units.tr: Between partners, indeed, these actions in common property are not given one partner against another; but they may be brought by the action for partition, by which one may claim not that the partner has the right to do work, but that he has no right to do it, or to do work, or, with the partner absent, to hold it so.

units.la: l. 26. in re communi D. de Seruit. prǣd. urb. l. 11. an unus. D. Si ser. uind.
units.tr: l. 26. in re communi D. de Seruit. prǣd. urb. l. 11. an unus. D. Si ser. uind.

units.la: l. 28. Sabinus. D. Com. diuid.
units.tr: l. 28. Sabinus. D. Com. diuid.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Heredibus autem, & in heredes hae Actiones dantur: (nō tamen iure successionis, sed eo iure quo Domini sunt:) idque in solidum, si plures sint: propter indiuiduam harum seruitutum naturam. aliud in Vsufr.
units.tr: These actions are given to heirs and against heirs (yet not by the right of succession, but by the right by which they are owners), and for the whole where there are several, on account of the indivisible nature of these servitudes. It is otherwise in usufruct.

units.la: {1} ita in Simili l. 42. §. D. de nox act. l. 1. §. D. Si quad. paup.
units.tr: {1} ita in Simili l. 42. §. D. de nox act. l. 1. §. D. Si quad. paup.

units.la: {2} l. 17. uiæ. D. de Seruit. l. 5. D. de Vsufr. l. 2. §. J. et Seq. l. 3. et 4. D. de Verb. oblig.
units.tr: {2} l. 17. uiæ. D. de Seruit. l. 5. D. de Vsufr. l. 2. §. J. et Seq. l. 3. et 4. D. de Verb. oblig.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Sic &, si prædium cui Seruitus debetur, plurium sit, vnicuique in solidum competit Actio : et contra , si plurium sit prædium quod seruit, aduersus unumquemq; poterit ita agi.
units.tr: So too, if the estate to which a servitude is owed belongs to several, the action lies for each of them for the whole; and conversely, if the estate that is burdened belongs to several, one may proceed in this way against each of them.

units.la: l. 4. §. 2. Si fundus. D. Si ser. uind.
units.tr: l. 4. §. 2. Si fundus. D. Si ser. uind.

units.la: XIIII.
units.tr: XIIII.

units.la: Lite autem ab uno de communi Seruitute instituta : vi-ctoria quidem & aliis proderit: offensio vero & causæ amissio, quæ culpa eius acciderit, ceteris damno esse non debet. Et si per collusionem cessit lite aduersario, ceteris dabitur Actio de dolo.
units.tr: If one of the co-owners of a common servitude has brought a suit, victory will benefit the others too; but defeat and loss of the case, which come through his fault, should not harm the rest. And if he yielded the case to the opponent through collusion, the others will be given an action for fraud.

units.la: d. §. Si fundus. l. 19[?]. Si de communi. D. Si ser. uind.
units.tr: d. §. Si fundus. l. 19[?]. Si de communi. D. Si ser. uind.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Venit porro in has Actiones ipsum Ius Seruitutis : habita tamen & damni, et fructuum, siue eius quod interest, ratione.
units.tr: Moreover, the right of servitude itself falls within these actions, though account is also taken of the loss, of the fruits, or of what is in the interest of the plaintiff.

units.la: l. 5. C. de Seruit. d. l. 4. §. 1[?]. l. 6. §. ult. D. Si ser. uind.
units.tr: l. 5. C. de Seruit. d. l. 4. §. 1[?]. l. 6. §. ult. D. Si ser. uind.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Quare agens Confessoria, probare debet ius sibi esse ire a-gere, altius tollendi, et Negatoria, ius alteri non esse.
units.tr: Hence the plaintiff in a confessory action must prove that he has the right to pass, to drive, or to raise his building higher; and in a negatory action, that the other has no such right.

units.la: arg. l. 5. uers. quamquam D. Si Vsusf. pet.
units.tr: arg. l. 5. uers. quamquam D. Si Vsusf. pet.

units.la: De Probationibus Seruitutum, negotium perdifficile.
units.tr: On the Proofs of Servitudes, a Very Difficult Matter.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Negatio enim, quæ non est mera, sed involutam & tacitam habet affirmationem, probari potest.
units.tr: For a denial, which is not bare but contains an implied and tacit affirmation, can be proved.

units.la: l. 8. Si filius. D. de. Probat.
units.tr: l. 8. Si filius. D. de Probat.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Ceterum, An præter Ius, qua de re agitur, aliud quoq; Actor probare debeat, ut prædij sui Dominium, vel Emphy-teusin, etc. tam in Cõfess. quam in Negat. iure et merito quæ-ri potest. Puto tamen debere: quamuis leges Seruitutis fere mentionem mentionem faciant.{2} idq; exemplo Hypothecariæ, in qua Creditor non tantum duo, ut hic, sed tria probare cogitur, debitum, pignus, et rem fuisse in bonis Debitoris tempore contrahendi pignoris.{3}
units.tr: Moreover, whether the plaintiff must also prove something beyond the right in question, such as ownership of his estate or emphyteusis, etc., can rightly and properly be asked both in the confessory and in the negatory action. I think, however, that he must, although the laws on servitude scarcely mention it. This is shown by analogy with the hypothecary action, in which the creditor is compelled to prove not only two things, as here, but three: the debt, the pledge, and that the thing was among the debtor's goods at the time the pledge was contracted.

units.la: 1. arg. eo, quod hæ Act. dantur domino et l. 5. ff. quod si forte. Si Vsusf.pe.
units.tr: 1. Argument from the fact that these actions are given to the owner, and l. 5. ff. quod si forte. Si Usufr. pet.

units.la: 2. l. 7. §. 9. C. de Seruit l. 9. et 10. D. si fer, uind.
units.tr: 2. l. 7. §. 9. C. de Servit. l. 9. and 10. D. Si fer. vind.

units.la: 3. l. 10. nec creditores. C. de pig. Act. l. 23. ante D. de probat l. 3. l. 15. et quæ, §. 1. D. de pigno.
units.tr: 3. l. 10, nor the creditors. C. de pig. Act. l. 23, before D. de probat. l. 3, l. 15, and what follows, §. 1, D. de pigno.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: Sunt qui putent, has Actiones, saltem utiles, non modo Seruitutum, sed etiam Vectigalium, & Imperij, siue Iurisdictionis, ut loquuntur, nomine dari posse, quibus non adsentior.{1} Ea enim quæ sunt iuris publici, ut Vectigalia. &c. non veniunt in priuatas Actiones.{2}
units.tr: There are those who think that these actions, at least as useful actions, can be granted not only in the name of servitudes but also of tolls and of jurisdiction, as they say, to which I do not assent. For those things which belong to public law, such as tolls, etc., do not come within private actions.

units.la: 1. ipse quoque. Accurf. et recentiores quidam, Corrasius, Vaudus id improbant. quorū hæc est ratio, quod hæ Act. de Seruitutibus Propositæ fuerunt in Edicto. eas autem alio producere, non esse interpretis, sed prætoris aut legis l. 5. §. 2. D. Si mens.fals.mod.
units.tr: 1. Accursius himself, and certain more recent writers, Corrasius and Vaudus, reject this. Their reason is that these actions concerning servitudes were set out in the Edict; but to extend them to other matters belongs not to the interpreter but to the praetor or the law. l. 5. §. 2. D. Si mens. fals. mod.

units.la: 2. §. ult. Inst. tit. et §. ult. tit. 2.
units.tr: 2. §. ult. Inst. tit. and §. ult. tit. 2.

units.la: XX.
units.tr: XX.

units.la: Quare nec eorum sententiam probare possum, qui hæc publica iura, vel Condict. Triticiaria, vel Act. præscr. verbis, vel Cõdict. certi, vel ex lege peti posse existimant. Potius Arbitrio utendum aliorum Principum, aut Rerumpub. ut videre est apud Cic. 1. de Offic. &c.
units.tr: Hence I cannot approve the opinion of those who think that these public rights may be claimed either by a condictio triticiaria, or by the praescriptis verbis action, or by a condictio certi, or from the law. Rather one must use the judgment of other princes or commonwealths, as can be seen in Cicero, 1. de Officiis, etc.

units.la: XXI.
units.tr: XXI.

units.la: Euentus harum Actionum est, ut victori Officio iudicis aut res præstetur, aut cautio, eaque nuda, sed varie, pro ratione rei aut petitionis. V.G. ut vindicans Seruitutem, victus, caueat caueat victori se Seruitute non usurum: negans, victus, caueat se Seruituti non fore impedimento.
units.tr: The outcome of these actions is that, with the judge's office in the winner's favour, either the thing is delivered or security is given, and that a bare security, but varying according to the nature of the thing or of the claim. For example, if the claimant of a servitude is defeated, he gives security to the winner that he will not use the servitude; if the denier is defeated, he gives security that he will not be an obstacle to the servitude.

units.la: XXII.
units.tr: XXII.

units.la: Videntur autem & hæ Actiones, ut ipsa Rei vindicatio, esse Arbitrariæ.
units.tr: These actions, however, like the vindication of the thing itself, seem to be arbitrary.

units.la: arg. l. 68. qui restituere. D. de Rei uind. d. l. 7. harum. D. Si ser. uind.
units.tr: arg. l. 68. qui restituere. D. de Rei vind. d. l. 7. harum. D. Si serv. vind.

units.la: XXIII.
units.tr: XXIII.

units.la: Reus igitur, Siquidem iussus aut rem præstare aut cautionem, iussui paruerit, absoluetur: Si vero non paruerit, tanti condemnabitur, quanti Actor in litem iurauerit.
units.tr: Therefore the defendant, if he has been ordered either to deliver the thing or to give security and obeys the order, will be absolved; but if he does not obey, he will be condemned for as much as the plaintiff swears to in litem.

units.la: d. l. 7. harum.
units.tr: d. l. 7. harum.

units.la: XXIIII.
units.tr: XXIV.

units.la: Quod si his Actionibus conuentus, se non defendat: partes Iudicis non aliæ erunt, quam ut cauere eum iubeat, non prius se, vel iure eo quo uti vellet, usurum, vel eo quo actor uti vult, eum non prohibiturum, quam de iure suo, aut utendi, aut prohibendi, intra tempus à Iudice præfinitum probarit. atq;ita ex reo fit actor, propter contumaciam: etiam ex possessore, non possessor.
units.tr: But if, when sued in these actions, the defendant does not defend himself, the judge's part will be nothing other than to order him to give security that he will not use the right he wished to use, or that he will not prohibit the plaintiff from using the right the plaintiff wishes to use, unless he proves his right either to use or to prohibit within the time fixed by the judge. And so the defendant becomes the plaintiff, on account of his contumacy; and the possessor, too, becomes not the possessor.

units.la: d. l. 15. Si priusquam. D. de op. no. nunt. l. 45. ab eo. D. de damn. inf.
units.tr: d. l. 15. Si priusquam. D. de op. no. nunt. l. 45. ab eo. D. de damn. inf.

units.la: XXV.
units.tr: XXV.

units.la: Ceterum, in possessionem quoq; ut Actor mittatur omnium bonorum non defendentis, inhumanum videtur: Latitantis, verum est.
units.tr: Moreover, that the plaintiff should be put into possession of all the goods of a defendant who does not defend himself seems inhuman; but of one who hides, it is true.

units.la: l. 7. Fulcinius §. Celsus. et. §. item uideamus. D. Quib. ex causs. in poss. l. 18. ie [?] cuius. D. Si ser. uind.
units.tr: l. 7. Fulcinius §. Celsus. et §. item videamus. D. Quib. ex causis in poss. l. 18. ie [?] cuius. D. Si serv. vind.

units.la: XXVI.
units.tr: XXVI.

units.la: Huc quoq; pertinet, quod eleganter ait Ulp. per Sententi-am non debere Seruitutem constitui, sed quae est declarari{1}: Sententia enim ius non facit. quod idem & in Dominio, et in Pignore, certum est{2}.
units.tr: To this also pertains what Ulpian elegantly says: that a servitude should not be constituted by a sentence, but should be declared to exist.{1} For a sentence does not create a right. This is certainly the same in ownership and in pledge.{2}

units.la: {1} l. 8. sicut. §. 3. Sed si quæritur. D. Si Ser. vind.
units.tr: {1} l. 8. sicut. §. 3. Sed si quaeritur. D. Si serv. vind.

units.la: {2} l. 35. etc. ex diverso. §. 1. D. de Rei vind. l. 3. D. d. pig.
units.tr: {2} l. 35. etc. ex diverso. §. 1. D. de Rei vind. l. 3. D. de pig.

units.la: XXVII.
units.tr: XXVII.

units.la: Plane id ipsum libello Admonitionis cōplecti, siue eo Judicem rogare, ut declaret Seruitutem, Dominium etc. ad Actorem pertinere, non est necesse. quamuis contra iam sit à pragmaticis usurpatum.
units.tr: Plainly, it is not necessary to include this very point in a libel of admonition, or to ask the judge to declare that the servitude or ownership etc. belongs to the plaintiff, although practitioners have already adopted the contrary practice.

units.la: XXVIII.
units.tr: XXVIII.

units.la: Quod autem supra initio dictum, Seruitutum nomine dari duas Actiones, Confessoriam, et Negatoriam: id in rebus Corporalibus receptum non est, in quibus nulla datur Negatoria.
units.tr: As for what was said at the beginning, that two actions, the confessory and the negatory, are granted in the name of servitudes: this is not accepted for corporeal things, in which no negatory action is granted.

units.la: d. §. Aeque.
units.tr: d. §. Aeque.

units.la: XXIX.
units.tr: XXIX.

units.la: Ratio huius differentiae est, quia in rebus Incorporalibus tam possidenti, quam non possidenti datur Actio: in Corporalibus tantum datur ei, qui non possidet.
units.tr: The reason for this difference is that in incorporeal things an action is granted both to the possessor and to the non-possessor; in corporeal things it is granted only to one who does not possess.

units.la: d. §. Aeque. l. 1. §-pe. D. Vti possi. l. 6. et si forte. §. 1. D. Si Ser. vind.

units.tr: XXX.

units.la: Jā, cur in Incorp. Actio detur quoq; possessori, in Corporalibus, nō detur, alij alias rationes adferunt: mihi hæc probatur, quod Seruitutes in usu, id est, in facto, quodam genere,
units.tr: Why, then, in incorporeal things an action is granted also to the possessor, but not in corporeal things, others give other reasons; to me this one is approved: that servitudes consist in use, that is, in a certain kind of act,

units.la: consistunt eostituunt[?]{1}: Dominium quo de agitur in rebus Corporal. est mere iuris: à quo Dominio perspicue separatur Possessio.{2}
units.tr: consist are constituted{1}: ownership, which is the subject in corporeal things, is purely a matter of right; from this ownership possession is clearly separated.{2}

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: Quare, cui Usus Servitutis impeditur, ipsa quodammodo Servitus impediri, aut in controversiam vocari videtur: at in rebus corpor. Possessio earum impediri aut inquietari potest, salvo licet & in controverso Dominio.
units.tr: Hence, when the use of a servitude is hindered, the servitude itself seems in some way to be hindered or called into question; but in corporeal things possession of them can be hindered or disturbed, even though ownership remains untouched and in dispute.

units.la: XXXII.
units.tr: XXXII.

units.la: Et hæc quoq; causa est, cur Præiudicia non dentur Pos-sessori: nempe, quod in causa Status, perspicue distinguatur Possessio à Proprietate.
units.tr: And this is also the reason why prejudicial actions are not granted to the possessor: namely, because in a question of status possession is clearly distinguished from ownership.

D. de probat, Glossographi Bartolum secuti distinguunt inter adfectiones naturales, et inpositcias[?], item inter eas quæ consentiant cum intentione actoris, ut loquuntur, et eas quæ non consentiant, quos et Comensis recte reprehendit ad d. l. Siprius. nu. 22.

The glossators, following Bartolus, distinguish between natural and imposed affections, and again between those which agree with the plaintiff's intention, as they say, and those which do not; which Comensis also rightly criticises at d. l. Si prius, n. 22.

units.la: XXXIII.
units.tr: XXXIII.

units.la: Quod autem modo dictum, in rebus Incorp. dari Actio-nem possidenti, ut Negatoriam: non ita accipiendum, quasi Negatoria soli possidenti detur, quam certum est dari et pos-sidenti, & non possidenti{3}, ut et Confessoriam{4}: Sed ob comparationem rerum Corp. facta possidentis tantum mentio. nam in iis dari Actionem possidenti, satis notum erat: non quidem negantem, id enim esset ibi absurdum, quia age-retur de iure alieno, sed aientem, sive Confessoriam.
units.tr: But what was just said, that in incorporeal things an action is granted to the possessor, namely the negatory, is not to be understood as if the negatory action were granted to the possessor alone; it is certain that it is granted both to the possessor and to the non-possessor,{3} as is also the confessory{4}. Rather, the mention of the possessor was made because of the comparison with corporeal things. For that an action is granted to the possessor in those things was well known; not, indeed, a denying one, for that would be absurd there, since the matter would concern another's right, but an affirming one, that is, the confessory.

units.la: Argumentatio Imp. in §. æque, uers. quod genus, etc. hæc est: Quæcumq; datur Actio possidenti, ea non datur in reb. Negatoria Actio datur possidenti. (Corp. Ergo Neg. non est prodita in reb. Corporal.
units.tr: The argument of the Emperor in §. Aeque, verse "quod genus", etc., is this: whatever action is granted to the possessor is not granted in respect of corporeal things; a negatory action is granted to the possessor. (Therefore the negatory action is not provided for in corporeal things.)

units.la: XXXIIII.
units.tr: XXXIV.

units.la: Sane uno casu Possessori Negatoriam in rebus Corporalibus, dari, quidam viri docti existimant{1}: eunq; casum, Alii{2} in causa Status, quod ia[?] refellimus: alij{3} in Interdicto Utipossidetis, in quo tamen, non de iure in rem, ex quo oritur Actio Cof. et Nega. sed de Possessione agitur: Alii{4} in d.l. si prius: quæ l. non de re Corporali, sed de Seruitute loquitur, ponunt.
units.tr: Certainly some learned men think that in one case a negatory action is granted to the possessor in corporeal things. Some take that case to be a matter of status, which we refute; others place it in the interdict Utipossidetis, in which, however, the question is not about a right in rem, from which the confessory and negatory actions arise, but about possession. Others place it in the law si prius, which speaks not of corporeal things but of servitude.

units.la: XXXV.
units.tr: XXXV.

units.la: Alii in Duplicibus iudicijs, Fa. erc. etc. Sed neq in his Actio datur possessori, & sunt mixtæ hæ Act. Alij² in eo qui ciuiliter possidens, ut Dominus, agit contra eum qui naturaliter tantum possideat, l. officium. D. de rei vind. Sed regula, qua dictum, possidenti non dari actionem, intelligenda est de eo qui rem corporaliter possidet: Alij³ in eo ponunt, qui conuentus Rei vindicatione, eam reuindicat, siue suam esse ait. sed hic neq agit, neq excipit, sed ait se esse dominum: Alij⁴[?] in l. 8. Papinianus. §. 13. Si Filius. D. de inoff. test. Sed ibi filius proprie non agit, ut et ipsi fatentur. quare κατὰ δ' ἐντιεσν ωλξν[?], adferunt idem, l.6. et si forte. §. 1. D. Si Seru. vind. Sed ibi de rebus Incorp. agitur: quaestio autem est de rebus Corp. Alij{4} deniq; de Exceptione aut praescriptione accipiunt. sed hoc neq; proprie est agere, & in plurimis casibus locum habet.
units.tr: Others place it in duplicate judgments, such as the familiae erciscundae and the like. But in these too no action is granted to the possessor, and these actions are mixed. Others place it in the case of one who, possessing civilly as owner, sues one who possesses only naturally (l. officium D. de rei vindicatione). But the rule that no action is granted to a possessor must be understood of one who possesses a thing corporeally. Others place it in the case of one who, sued by a vindication, claims the thing back, saying it is his own; but here he neither sues nor excepts, he says that he is the owner. Others cite l. 8, Papinianus, §13, Si filius, D. de inofficioso testamento. But there the son does not properly sue, as they themselves admit. Hence they bring forward the same thing from l. 6, et si forte, §1, D. Si servitus vindicetur. But there the matter concerns incorporeal things, whereas the question concerns corporeal things. Others finally take it as an exception or a prescription. But this is not properly to sue, and it applies in very many cases.

units.la: XXXVI.
units.tr: XXXVI.

units.la: Contra, sunt Viri doctiss.{1} qui multos casus esse putent, in quibus Possessor partes Actoris sustineat, quamuis Actor non sit, ut sunt aliquot in priori thesi expositi. idem q; pro, Sane uno casu, rescribunt, Sane non uno casu. Sed neq; ea distinctio, inter Actore, & Actoris partes sustinente, probabilis videtur{2}: et articulus, Sane, est index Exceptionis: at Regula fuit de Actore. ergo & Exceptio esse debet. nullus quoq; reperitur liber scriptus, in quo negatio extet.
units.tr: On the other hand, there are most learned men who think that there are many cases in which the possessor sustains the part of the plaintiff although he is not the plaintiff, as several are set out in the previous thesis. They also read the same for "Sane uno casu" as "Sane non uno casu". But that distinction, between a plaintiff and one who sustains the part of a plaintiff, does not seem probable; and the word "Sane" is a sign of exception, whereas the rule was about the plaintiff. Therefore the exception must be so too. Nor is any written book found in which the negation stands.

units.la: {1} Aemil. Ferret. ad d. §. æque. a quo non longe discedit & Duaren. ad tit. de Probat. cap. 33. et D. Donell. hic. licet Ferretus à scipse dissentiat, teste Charonda[?] d cap. 1.
units.tr: {1} Aemilius Ferretus on the said §. aeque, from whom Duaren on the title de probationibus, cap. 33, and D. Donellus here do not differ much, although Ferretus himself disagrees, as Charondas attests on cap. 1.

units.la: {2} Petitoris aut actoris partes, uel onera sustinere, aut fungit de eo dici solet, qui probare cogitur, ut actor. quod cognosci poterit ex l. 8. §. 3. Sed si quaeritur. D. Si Ser. uind. l. 62. inter. D. de iudic. l. pe. D. de Carb. ed. l. 7. liber l. 35. §. ulti. D. de lib. caus. l' ult. D. Si ing. l. 35. exitus. D. de adq. poss. l. 1. §. 2. D. Vti, poss.
units.tr: {2} To sustain the part or burdens of a petitioner or plaintiff, or to act, is said of one who is compelled to prove, as a plaintiff is. This can be recognised from l. 8, §3, Sed si quaeritur, D. Si servitus vindicetur; l. 62, inter, D. de iudiciis; l. pe. D. de carboniano edicto; l. 7, liber; l. 35, §ult. D. de libera causa; l. ult. D. Si ingenuus; l. 35, exitus, D. de adquirenda possessione; l. 1, §2, D. Utipossidetis.

units.la: XXXVII.
units.tr: XXXVII.

units.la: Sunt deniq; item egregij Jurisconf. qui fatentur quidem nullum nullũ esse casum, quo in reb. Corp. detur Actio possidenti, sed putant eum uerf. Sane uno casu, de Seruitutibus accipiendum. Sed eos refellit cum ipse articulus Sane, index Exceptionis aut noui casus: idq; et τὸ[?] uno, et τὸ[?] nihilominus indicatum inutilis esset iteratio eius, quod modo dictum fuerat.
units.tr: There are, finally, also some distinguished jurists who indeed admit that there is no case in which an action is granted to the possessor in corporeal things, but think that the phrase "Sane uno casu" must be taken of servitudes. But they are refuted, since the word "Sane", an indicator of an exception or a new case, and "uno" and "nihilominus" show that its repetition would be pointless, given what had just been said.

units.la: 1. Baro, Hotom. Cuiac. ad d. § æque. et hic ad d. l. Si prius, pro, et Illi uno, leg. putant, in hoc, uel illo.
units.tr: 1. Baro, Hotomannus, Cujacius on the said §. aeque, and here on the said l. Si prius, who think that for "et illi uno" one should read "in hoc, vel illo".

units.la: XXXVIII.
units.tr: XXXVIII.

units.la: Quare cum hic ver. Sane uno casu, iuri, & rationi, atque adeo huic § repugnet, nec ulla ex eo sententia idonea & vera elici possit: Videndum, ne rectius, ea verba, Sane &c. obtinet, induci debeant. Quod neq; in libris iuris nouum videri debet, et in aliis scriptoribus saepe est obseruatum{2}.
units.tr: Therefore, since here the phrase "Sane uno casu" conflicts with law, with reason, and indeed with this §, and no sound and true sentence can be drawn from it, it must be considered whether it is rather those words, "Sane" and so on, that ought to be removed. This should not seem new in law books, and it has often been observed in other writers.

Faber thinks those words in "Hac epistola", l. 1, §ult. D. de quaestionibus, and so on, should be removed; Cujacius those in the Collationes, and so on, l. 11 C. de legatis, heredibus instituendis.

units.la: XXXIX.
units.tr: XXXIX.

units.la: Hactenus de Actionibus Seruitutum. Sunt autem & alia de his remedia. nam et Noui operis nuntiatio habenti Seruitutem, sed Vrbanam, permittitur: et Interdicta quasi possessoria, Seruitutum nomine constituta sunt{2}. ut alia auxilia de damno omittam, ut Stip. damn. inf. Act. in factum{3}.
units.tr: So far concerning the actions of servitudes. There are, however, other remedies besides these. For both the notice of new work is permitted to one who has a servitude, though an urban one, and interdicts quasi-possessory are established in the name of servitudes. To pass over other aids for damage, such as the stipulation for threatened damage and the action in factum.

units.la: XXXX.
units.tr: XL.

units.la: Et Siquidem quasi possidet quis ius Servitutis: utilior est ei vel Actio, vel Interdictum, quam Noui op. nunt. eo quod is qui hac utitur, adversarium faciat possessorem: qui illis, nō item{1}. Interdictum quoq; Actione est commodius, quia in illo, fere de facto, in hac agitur de iure{2}, quod est difficilius ad probandum. Si vero quis non est in possessione: optima est Nuntiatio, ut quae statim, nō adito quoq; Praetore, opus inhibeat{3}. Sed non semper locus est Nuntiationi.
units.tr: And if anyone quasi-possesses a right of servitude, an action or an interdict is more useful to him than the notice of new work, because the one who uses it makes his adversary a possessor, which the other does not. The interdict is also more convenient than the action, because in the former the matter is almost one of fact, whereas in the latter it is one of right, which is harder to prove. But if someone is not in possession, the notice is best, since it at once inhibits the work, even without approaching the praetor. Yet notice does not always have a place.

units.la: XXXXI.
units.tr: XLI.

units.la: Illud his adiciendum, Servitutum nomine non modo Actionem, sed etiam Exceptionem possidenti dari: et utroq; auxilio uti eum posse qui Servitutem quasi possidet{1}. Cui enim damus Actionem, eidem & Exceptionem competere multo magis quis dixerit{2}.
units.tr: To these let this be added: that in the name of servitudes not only an action but also an exception is given to the possessor, and that he who quasi-possesses a servitude may use both aids. For one would say, much more readily, that an exception is also available to the person to whom we grant an action.

units.tr: Exceptions that can be raised against these actions are a common matter, such as those of agreement and of fraud, though most especially those of time.

units.la: XLII.
units.tr: XLII.

units.la: Vix operae est admonere, Ea quae adhuc dicta sunt de Actionibus Servitutum nomine, accipienda esse de Servitutibus iam constitutis siue ipso iure, siue tuitione Prætoris: Nam de promissis aut venditis tantum, nec dum cōstitutis, ut eæ imponantur, competunt Actiones in personam, ut Condictio incerti, vel Actio ex empto. {s}
units.tr: It is scarcely necessary to remind the reader that what has been said so far about the actions named after servitudes must be understood of servitudes already established, whether by law itself or by the protection of the praetor. For actions in personam, such as the condictio incerti or the actio ex empto, lie only for promised or sold servitudes that are not yet established, so that they may be imposed.

units.la: XXXX III.
units.tr: XLIII.

units.la: Ex his facile iam est, & Definitionem harum Actionū elicere, u.g. Confessoria est Actio Ciuilis in rem, qua Seruitus prædij vindicatur: & Formulā siue Libellum: cuius non quatuor sunt capita, ut pragmatici numerant, sed unum hoc princeps, quo Actor dicat, tale ius ad se pertinere, vel neget, alteri tale ius esse, ut eundi, altius tollendi: cui capiti accedere potest, ut dicat, Actor se in suo illo iure per hunc impediri.
units.tr: From these points it is now easy to draw out the definitions of these actions. For example, the confessoria is a civil action in rem, by which a servitude of an estate is claimed. Its formula, or libellus, does not have four heads, as the practical writers count them, but this one principal head, by which the plaintiff says that such a right (of passage, or of building higher) belongs to him, or the defendant denies that the other party has such a right. To this head may be added that the plaintiff says he is hindered by this man in that his right.

units.la: Parerga.
units.tr: Miscellanies

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Successorem Regni, aut Ciuitatis, teneri æs alienum, ab An-tecessore, publico aut Reip. nomine contractum, dissoluere.
units.tr: The successor to a kingdom or a commonwealth is bound to discharge a debt contracted by his predecessor in the name of the public or the commonwealth.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Magistratum, qui vel sontem, ut latronem, vel hostem per-secutus in alieni iuris vicino & non hostili territorio ceperit, restituere eum Magistratui aut Principi eius loci debere: & hoc amplius, de iniuria eidem satisfacere.
units.tr: A magistrate who, having pursued a criminal, such as a robber, or an enemy, captures him in the territory of a neighbouring state that is not hostile and belongs to another's jurisdiction, ought to restore him to the magistrate or prince of that place, and moreover to make satisfaction to that same party for the injury.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Quamuis Proportionum tres adferantur species, Arithme-tica, Geometrica, & Harmonica: Recte tamen ab Aristotele Iustitiam in duas tantum species tributam videri, Permutatio-nis, & Diuisionis. IIII.
units.tr: Although three kinds of proportion are cited, arithmetical, geometrical and harmonic, nevertheless Aristotle rightly holds that justice is divided into only two kinds, that of exchange and that of distribution. IIII.

units.la: Recte à Veteribus à Baptismo Christi ad eius mortem nu-merari quatuor tantum Paschata.
units.tr: Rightly the Fathers reckon only four Passovers from the baptism of Christ to his death.
